title: Thieves hijack AI hardware shipments in California
content:
Cargo thieves ram security escorts to hijack AI hardware shipments in California — brazen thieves employ PIT maneuver, rear-ending tactics to secure goods for the black market
Stolen AI hardware can now fetch more than its U.S. retail price overseas.
Cargo thieves knocked two private security escort vehicles out of action on California roads in recent months, then made off with millions of dollars in AI data center hardware the escorts were guarding, according to a WIRED investigation. Both shipments were traveling from Silicon Valley to Southern California, and neither truck has been recovered. The attacks come as cargo theft losses across the U.S. and Canada more than doubled year over year to $304.6 million in Q2 2026, and as restricted Nvidia servers sell in China for roughly twice their U.S. retail price.
Gerardo Pachuca, a former Los Angeles sheriff's detective who now consults on cargo crime, told WIRED that one escort was rear-ended by a driver who fled the scene, while the other was spun off the road with a PIT maneuver, the same tactic police use to end car chases. Once the escorts were disabled, the semitrucks kept driving and disappeared. Investigators believe the truck drivers were complicit, with both thefts involving motor carrier numbers that had recently changed hands, a fraud technique that lets criminals book freight under a legitimate company's federal registration. "It's the worst I've seen," Pachuca said of cargo theft nationwide.
WIRED couldn't confirm the incidents with five state and local law enforcement agencies, but two freight security figures corroborated them: J.J. Coughlin, chairman of the Southwest Transportation Security Council, and Danny Ramon, director of intelligence and response at freight-monitoring firm Overhaul.
Verisk CargoNet documented 677 supply chain theft incidents in the U.S. and Canada in Q2 2026, down 26% from a year earlier, yet estimated losses jumped from $135.7 million to $304.6 million over the same period, according to a recent report by the firm. The average theft with a reported value hit $564,009. "Lower incident volume should not be mistaken for lower risk," said Keith Lewis, vice president of operations at Verisk CargoNet.
Enterprise computing and networking equipment ranks among the most targeted categories, and Verisk noted that shipments worth several million dollars routinely move as conventional dry freight with no special security. Recoveries this summer included $550,000 in Celestica-built server switches destined for Meta and roughly $1 million in data center equipment found in a trailer outside Chicago.
Freight investigators, including Pachuca, told WIRED that location pings from stolen components suggest many shipments end up overseas. Stolen cargo normally fences at a steep discount, but U.S. export controls have pushed black market prices in China far above American retail: Nvidia's DGX B300 server sells there for more than $1.1 million against a U.S. price of roughly $550,000, and even five-year-old A100 servers have tripled in price. A hijacked truckload of restricted AI hardware is one of the few categories of stolen goods that can be worth more on the black market than off of it.

report.summary: Thieves used PIT maneuvers to disable security escorts and hijack millions in AI data center hardware in California, driven by soaring black-market demand.
report.background: Cargo theft has surged as AI data center hardware becomes scarce and valuable. U.S. export controls bar advanced Nvidia servers from China, where restricted systems sell for roughly twice U.S. retail—DGX B300 over $1.1M vs $550K. Thieves use fake motor carrier numbers, rear-ending and PIT maneuvers to disable escorts. Verisk CargoNet recorded 677 incidents in Q2 2026, down 26%, but losses doubled to $304.6M, average $564K. Enterprise computing and networking gear are top targets, often shipped as ordinary dry freight without security. Investigators say location pings suggest many stolen shipments end up overseas, making hijacked AI hardware uniquely profitable on the black market.
key_points: Two hijackings in California saw security escorts disabled by rear-end and PIT maneuvers; the semitrucks and millions in AI data center hardware disappeared. Investigators believe drivers were complicit, using recently changed motor carrier numbers to fraudulently book freight under legitimate registrations.

Losses are soaring even as incident counts fall: Q2 2026 had 677 supply chain thefts in the U.S. and Canada, down 26% year over year, yet losses jumped from $135.7M to $304.6M. The average theft with reported value hit $564,009.

Black market economics are inverted: U.S. export controls make restricted Nvidia servers sell in China for far above U.S. retail. DGX B300 servers fetch over $1.1M versus $550K in the U.S., and even five-year-old A100 servers have tripled in price.

High-value shipments often move with little protection. Enterprise computing and networking gear ranks among the most targeted categories, and multi-million-dollar loads routinely travel as conventional dry freight. Recoveries included $550K in Celestica server switches for Meta and $1M in data center gear near Chicago.

Investigators say location pings from stolen components point to overseas destinations, indicating organized theft rings targeting AI hardware specifically to exploit export-control gaps and resell at premium black-market prices.
report.impact: The attacks highlight a growing security crisis in the AI supply chain. For the AI industry, hardware theft raises insurance, escort, and logistics costs, and may delay data center buildouts. Developers could face higher component prices, longer lead times, and stricter verification for second-hand or gray-market hardware. Regular users may ultimately see higher cloud and AI service costs if providers pass on security and replacement expenses. The incidents also pressure regulators to tighten export controls and freight oversight, while law enforcement may prioritize cargo crime. Ultimately, the black-market premium on restricted AI hardware turns ordinary freight routes into high-stakes targets, requiring coordinated industry, insurer, and government response.
report.tools: For tracking and risk analytics, watch Overhaul, Verisk CargoNet, Samsara, project44, and FourKites. Flock Safety provides license plate recognition for investigations. Open Supply Hub and OpenSanctions offer open resources for supply chain mapping and entity vetting. For hardware authenticity, Nvidia serial number verification and tamper-evident asset tags are increasingly important. These tools help shippers monitor loads, vet carriers, and trace stolen components.
